prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.

Your job is not to translate the diff. Make those changes.

- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.

- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

One or more of them may have changed since Swedish was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current Swedish page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the Swedish page up to date with the current English page: find what it says that Swedish does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the Swedish page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish states it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when Swedish says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder Swedish.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

One or more of them may have changed since Swedish was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current Swedish page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the Swedish page up to date with the current English page: find what it says that Swedish does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the Swedish page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish states it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when Swedish says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder Swedish.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Markup is not text. You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

One or more of them may have changed since Swedish was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current Swedish page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the Swedish page up to date with the current English page: find what it says that Swedish does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the Swedish page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish states it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when Swedish says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder Swedish.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Markup is not text. prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions (Swedish (sv)). The languages are equal peers; none is the original. One or more of them may have changed since English was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current English page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the English page up to date with the current Swedish page: find what it says that English does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the English page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in English: everywhere English states it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when English says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder English.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: every place where the English page no longer says what the other pages say, quoted from both, with whether you think it is a change waiting to be made in English or a difference on purpose, and why.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since English was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since English was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

import { CmButton } from '@acme/blocks/CmButton';
import { CmColumn, CmColumns } from '@acme/blocks/CmColumns';
import { CmFeatureRow } from '@acme/blocks/CmFeatureRow';
import { CmHero } from '@acme/blocks/CmHero';
import { CmSection } from '@acme/blocks/CmSection';
import { TextBlock } from '@acme/blocks/TextBlock';

<CmHero id="hero-a1b2c3d4"
  title="Acme"
  subtitle="Acme is the world's best tournament system for the world's best tournaments"
  ctaText="Learn more about Acme"
  ctaLink="/en/missa-inte/"
  backgroundMedia="/media/start-video-002-optimized.mp4"
  poster="/media/home/hero-poster.jpg"
/>

<CmSection id="sect-e5f6a7b8"
  heading="What is Acme?"
  contain="true"
  align="left"
  body={"Acme helps you as a tournament organiser deliver a smooth, fantastic overall experience to your participants. From registration, payment, draws and match schedules to live reporting of goals and final results on the web, in mobile apps or via SMS.\n\nWe've made it simple for tournaments of every size and complexity, big or small."}
  divider={true}
  contained={true}
/>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-2c8d91e4"
  eyebrow="Smarter scheduling with AI"
  title="How it works in Acme"
  ctaText="Read more about AI in Acme here"
  ctaLink="/en/vara-ai-losningar/"
  image="/media/home/ai-image-copy-1.webp"
  imageAlt="AI scheduling in Acme"
  imagePosition="left"
  bgColor="white"
>
  Building a match schedule that actually works is a complex puzzle – especially with hundreds or thousands of matches, multiple venues, rest periods and special requests to consider.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-7f04b3a9"
  eyebrow="CASE STUDY: FJORDBY BASKET FESTIVAL"
  title="One of our customers shares their story"
  ctaText="Read about Fjordby Basket Festival here"
  ctaLink="/en/fjordby-basket-festival/"
  image="/media/home/customer-story.png"
  imageAlt="Fjordby Basket Festival"
  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"
>
  Read our feature on a successful journey for basketball and Fjordby, Norway. Ola Nordvik talks about their journey – how they've grown, what they've achieved, and the new goals they keep setting for their tournament's future.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-91d5c0e7"
  eyebrow="WE'RE PROUD OF OUR SUPPORT"
  title="World-class support"
  ctaText="Read more about our support here"
  ctaLink="/en/support/"
  image="/media/home/support.webp"
  imageAlt="The Acme support team"
  imagePosition="left"
  bgColor="white"
>
  Perhaps the most defining part of Acme is our support. Everyone at the company works with one ultimate goal: helping our customers. We're available every day to help you with everything from quick questions to hands-on assistance with match schedules and planning advice.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-4a6e82d1"
  eyebrow="SIMPLE PAYMENT SOLUTIONS"
  title="Accept card, Klarna or Swish payments with ease"
  ctaText="Read more about our payment solution"
  ctaLink="/en/kort-och-klarna/"
  image="/media/home/klarna_acme-3.webp"
  imageAlt="Payment with Klarna in Acme"
  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"
  imageFocus="left center"
>
  Our modern payment solution means you can skip bank transfers entirely. Let teams pay by card or Klarna, so payments are registered automatically in the system and the money lands in your account right away.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-c3b90f52"
  eyebrow="ENGAGE YOUR VISITORS"
  title="Your own mobile app for Android and iPhone"
  ctaText="Get an app for your tournament"
  ctaLink="/en/app/"
  image="/media/home/usp-mobile-app.jpg"
  imageAlt="A dedicated mobile app for the tournament"
  imagePosition="left"
  bgColor="white"
>
  We can help you get your own mobile app for the tournament. We handle all the development, and the app connects directly to your tournament in Acme, so you can manage everything from one place.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmBandHeading id="band-5e17d8f0"
  heading="More information for the interested"
  bg="white"
  align="left"
  contained={true}
/>

<CmColumns id="cols-8b2f47c6"
  align="left"
  columns="2"
  gap="48"
  maxWidth={1140}
>
  <CmColumn id="col-d94a10e3"
    heading="Key features"
  >
    <TextBlock id="text-6c58e2b7">
      Don't miss our other great features, including live results, live streaming, a dedicated tournament website, accommodation & catering, referees, SMS notifications and check-in.
    </TextBlock>
    <CmButton id="btn-31f7a9d0"
      label="Read more about our features"
      href="/en/missa-inte/"
      variant="green"
      icon="none"
    />
  </CmColumn>
  <CmColumn id="col-59a3e8d7"
    heading="Pricing"
  >
    <TextBlock id="text-c21f80b4">
      We keep pricing simple, with a model that works for tournaments large and small across every sport. On top of a team-based licence, there's a range of optional extra services to choose from.
    </TextBlock>
    <CmButton id="btn-e40b97c3"
      label="Read more about our pricing"
      href="/en/priser/"
      variant="green"
      icon="none"
    />
  </CmColumn>
</CmColumns>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-06c9e3b8"
  eyebrow="COLLECT PAYMENTS FOR YOUR CLUB"
  title="Acme Clubs"
  ctaText="Read more about Acme Clubs"
  ctaLink="https://clubs.acme.example/"
  image="/media/home/si.jpg"
  imageAlt="Acme Clubs"
  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"
>
  Our sister product Acme Clubs is used by close to 1,000 clubs across Norway and Sweden to collect training fees and membership dues. It lets you tailor your collection to your needs while staying easy to use.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-f15b72a0"
  eyebrow="SPORT MATTERS IN A GLOBAL WORLD"
  title="Community, hope and growth – both at home and in East Africa."
  ctaText="Read more about the partnership"
  ctaLink="/en/lakeside-youth-cup/"
  image="/media/home/LakesideYouthCup.webp"
  imageAlt="Lakeside Youth Cup"
  imagePosition="left"
  bgColor="light"
>
  We partner with the Lakeside Youth Cup (LYC), an annual youth festival in Tanzania that empowers young people through sport, education and community engagement.
</CmFeatureRow>

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since English was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions (Swedish (sv)). The languages are equal peers; none is the original. One or more of them may have changed since English was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current English page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the English page up to date with the current Swedish page: find what it says that English does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the English page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in English: everywhere English states it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when English says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder English.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: every place where the English page no longer says what the other pages say, quoted from both, with whether you think it is a change waiting to be made in English or a difference on purpose, and why.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions (Swedish (sv)). The languages are equal peers; none is the original. One or more of them may have changed since English was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current English page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the English page up to date with the current Swedish page: find what it says that English does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the English page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in English: everywhere English states it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when English says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder English.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: every place where the English page no longer says what the other pages say, quoted from both, with whether you think it is a change waiting to be made in English or a difference on purpose, and why.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the English page up to date with the current Swedish page: find what it says that English does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the English page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in English: everywhere English states it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when English says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder English.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.
